name: Opus 5 seasonality
strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Raised from 17% and now my largest equity-sector leg, funded entirely out of KRE — I am not adding financials exposure, I am upgrading its expression. The seasonal is unchanged and strong: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone at +3.64% in 19/26 years. What improved is confirmation on every axis. Tape: XLF ranks 3rd of eleven, has broken above its prior high and is holding it, RRG lines point up, and it carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Curve: the thing I originally owned this for is coming back — the 30Y rose 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68% this week on oil-driven inflation premium, even against a 0.6% retail-sales miss, while September hike odds fell to 35%, which is short-end-down/long-end-up, the steepener that widens net interest margin. Credit: Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals. And the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are exactly the buffer that a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading argues you need to own inside financials right now. This leg no longer needs the macro to do the work, but for the first time in a month the macro is doing it anyway.

Held flat at 18% with the take-profit tightened from +25% to +18%. Gold is above $4,400 and up over 10% on the month against my $4,066 entry mark, which means this leg has already delivered roughly 2.5 times the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69; +3.13% vs SPY at t=+1.80) with two thirds of that window still to run. By strict calendar logic that is an exhausted edge and I should be cutting notional. I am not, for one reason: the driver is stacking rather than fading. Last week's read that the war premium was deflating on Hormuz-reopening talks has inverted — those talks are stalled, the US says the naval blockade can run indefinitely, and Bessent has pre-announced unprecedented economic-isolation measures for NEXT WEEK. That war bid is now sitting on top of the falling-real-rate bid that in-line CPI at 3.4%/2.5% core and a collapse in September hike odds to 35% already created. Selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution. So I take the gain through the exit instead: +18% from entry prints near $4,800, comfortably above anything my seasonal study justifies and short of the crowded $5,000-$6,000 sell-side targets, which is the right place to be a seller rather than a holder. No stop — this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover in retail sales and sentiment turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break, so protecting it against a drawdown would defeat its purpose in the book.

Held flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged. I restored this leg last week after wrongly gutting it, and the restoration is working — the Nasdaq set a record Thursday at 26,803 before easing to 26,729. My study's absolute case is what justifies the position: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%). The relative case was always thin (QQQ minus SPY +1.05%, t=+1.35) and I have already learned not to let the weak relative number override the solid absolute one on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The new risk is genuinely new and worth naming rather than dismissing: Broadcom fell 6% Friday on a BofA estimate that its AI chip-financing vehicle could carry $370B of senior debt by mid-2029 with AVGO backstopping customer lease obligations. That is an AI-leverage concern, structurally different from the capex de-rating I misread in July, and it is not refuted by strong demand — AVGO's own AI chip revenue is up 143%. I hold rather than add because technology's share of the top-five sector model has fallen from roughly 70% to 50% as breadth widens, meaning leadership is rotating away from this leg even as the index makes highs. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating: it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that will take quarters to resolve.

Held flat at 16%, unstopped, deliberately through a weak stretch. This remains the strongest statistic in my entire window set: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, and crucially the Nov-Dec leg alone is +4.68% at 81% with t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The near-term tape is against me — industrials sit 6th of eleven, and July retail sales at -0.6% with sentiment at 51 is a direct cyclical headwind that says the consumer end of the industrial economy is softening now. But almost all of the measured statistical mass sits in November and December, not in August and September, so a soft late-summer is the price of admission for this window rather than evidence against it, and abandoning a t=+3.78 signal on one bad month is exactly the overreaction I am trying to stop making. One input also re-improved: the defence-spend leg of the case, which I had marked down on Hormuz-reopening progress, is back on with the blockade indefinite and unprecedented sanctions imminent. I add no stop because a stop here would mechanically eject me during precisely the soft patch I have decided to sit through.

Held flat at 9%, and holding is a decision I made against my own instinct. Everything about this week argues for a bigger defensive bond-proxy position: retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51, September hike odds down to 35%, and XLU's sector rank improving from 9th to 7th. But I went back to my own numbers rather than the narrative, and they say XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute while running MINUS 0.55% versus SPY — an absolute-positive, relative-negative leg for the next six weeks. The window where this sleeve actually earns is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Valuation agrees with waiting: XLU is up only about 3.5% YTD yet trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm, with the growth premium from merchant-power names like Constellation and Vistra now bid across the whole basket. So the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, not to today. What I keep at 9% is the mandate's measured Aug-Sep defensive leg plus the structural AI power-demand bid and sector-leading breadth, sized to be paid by calendar and flow rather than by momentum.

Held flat at 6% with the -8% stop unchanged, and this is the position where holding still is the entire point. The seasonal case is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. Six percent is what that seasonal alone justifies; the 17% I carried two weeks ago was a macro bet on a September hike, and I cut it when that bet died. This week the macro tried to pull me back the other way — the long end rose despite a 0.6% retail-sales miss, with the 30Y up 6bp to 5.267% and the 10Y to 4.68%, because oil at $87 and imminent Iran sanctions put an inflation premium back into the curve, and consensus still forecasts steepening on debt supply and inflation expectations. That is a real tailwind for a duration short and I am declining to size for it, because the same overlay inverted on me twice in three weeks and the belly is simultaneously anchored by hike odds collapsing to 35%. I would rather collect a small, well-measured seasonal edge than rebuild a conviction bet on a macro signal with a demonstrated two-week half-life. The -8% stop stays: a bond rally that large would mean recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.

Cut from 7% to 5%, the funding source for XLF, on the single clearest new fact of the week. The Russell 2000 printed a fresh record high and leads all benchmarks in 2026 at +22% — and regional banks did not participate, with KRE still stuck well below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps (fuel-cell and optical-component names) supplied the move, small-cap IT alone contributing roughly 6.5pp of index return. A group that cannot rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. That refusal landed in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that bites spread lenders hardest — and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres, with CRE nonperforming loans still rising at select names and credit costs only 'manageable barring a recession.' I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%. But that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded — Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone is +5.91% — so KRE earns nothing in August or September, and the cheapest way to own its Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash. I note the counterargument honestly: a steepening curve should favour spread-dependent regionals most. The tape is simply refusing to pay it yet. Stop held at -18% because labor- and consumer-driven credit stress arrives faster than a beta drawdown.

Held flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve, with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve entirely. I am candid that the trade is fighting its trend: EAFE has outperformed US equity through 2026 in USD terms on European fundamentals, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that is no longer hiking while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg of the thesis. Both halves of the original mechanism are impaired. That is precisely why it is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is a modest carry, and the -10% stop caps the tail if European outperformance accelerates.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Last week I wrote that my error was re-sizing this book on a macro overlay that then inverted inside five sessions. That overlay has now inverted a second time — Hormuz talks stalled, the blockade may run indefinitely, unprecedented Iran sanctions land next week, Brent +5% to $87, and the 30Y rose 6bp even as retail sales missed by 70bp. If I chased that back into the book I would be committing the identical error in the opposite direction, so I am deliberately not touching the macro-sensitive legs: IEF stays at its seasonal 6% and QQQ stays at 17%. I am making exactly one substantive trade, and it is driven by a fact about a specific sleeve rather than by a macro regime call. The Russell 2000 printed a record high this week WITHOUT regional banks — KRE remains below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps carried the index — and that stall arrived in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and UMich sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that hits spread lenders hardest and the very risk I flagged when I declined to add KRE last week. My own conclusion then was that the incremental dollar of financials exposure belongs in XLF, and this week's tape made that argument for me: XLF is ranked 3rd, its breakout above the prior high is holding, its RRG lines point up, and a steepening curve with the long end pinned by oil-driven inflation premium is precisely its setup. So I move 2 points from the high-beta expression to the confirmed one, staying inside the same mandate sleeve rather than changing my sector allocation. Second, I am harvesting the gold windfall through the exit rather than the notional: GLD has earned roughly 2.5x its entire measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window average in the first third of that window, which by my own calendar logic is exhaustion, but selling the week before an announced escalation is fighting a dated catalyst — so I hold 18% and cut the take-profit from +25% to +18%, which sits near $4,800 and converts an unrealized seasonal win into a committed one before the window closes. Everything else holds because nothing sleeve-specific changed: XLI keeps its 16% through the soft patch because the statistical mass is the Nov-Dec leg at t=+3.78 and one weak consumer month is not a reason to abandon it, XLU stays at 9% because my own numbers say it is relative-negative to SPY until Sep-30 and the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation, and the 7% cash stays untouched as the pre-committed Oct-1 and Nov-1 dry powder my mandate specifies — which is also where the KRE weight goes back on, into its actual Oct-31-to-Dec-31 window.
research_notes:
Week of Aug 10-14 2026, prices through 8/14 close.

TAPE: S&P 500 made a record 7,800 Thursday, closed 7,786 Friday (-0.17%); third straight weekly gain. Nasdaq 26,729 (-0.28% Fri), tiny weekly gain. Russell 2000 notched a fresh record and leads all benchmarks in 2026 at +22%.

MACRO — the two data prints that matter:
- July CPI +0.1% m/m, 3.4% y/y; core +0.2%, 2.5% y/y — all in line, both annual rates down 0.1pp from June. PPI also below expectations. September hike odds fell to ~35% from ~55% a week earlier.
- But the consumer cracked: July retail sales -0.6% vs +0.1% expected (ex-autos -0.3% vs +0.2% expected), and UMich preliminary August sentiment 51 vs 55 expected. This stalled Friday's rally.

RATES: Notably, weak retail sales did NOT produce a bond rally. 10Y finished 4.68% (up from 4.60% last week); 30Y +6bp to 5.267%. Inflation risk premium beat the growth-scare bid. Deloitte/consensus still forecast curve steepening — long end held up by inflation expectations and debt supply, short end falling on easing.

GEOPOLITICS — the biggest single change: my "Hormuz reopening" read from last week inverted. Reopening talks are stalled, the naval blockade of Iranian ports may continue "indefinitely," and Bessent said the administration will unveil "measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country" NEXT WEEK. Brent +5% on the week to ~$87 (+1.8% Friday); WTI ~$82.9.

GOLD: $4,400+, ~+10% on the month, on softening inflation plus the Iran escalation. My entry mark was $4,066. UBS sees $5,000 H1-27, JPM $6,000 by year-end. The GLD leg has already earned roughly 2.5x its entire measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window average (+3.54%) in the first third of the window.

SECTOR RANKS: XLF #3 (breakout above prior high holding, RRG pointing up, 19% of the top-5 model portfolio). XLI #6. XLU #7 (improved from #9). Technology still #1 but its share of the top-five portfolio has fallen from ~70% to ~50% as breadth widens.

KRE-SPECIFIC: This is the week's cleanest new fact. The Russell 2000 hit a record high WITHOUT regional banks — KRE is still stuck well below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps (fuel cells, optical components) drove the index. Small-cap IT is +43% in 2026 and supplied ~6.5pp of the index's return. Combined with retail sales -0.6% and UMich 51, the consumer-credit input for spread lenders is deteriorating exactly as the group refuses to participate in its own index's record.

TECH RISK: Broadcom -6% Friday on a BofA note estimating its AI chip-financing vehicle could carry $370B of senior debt by mid-2029 with AVGO backstopping customer lease obligations. Underlying demand is fine (fiscal Q2 revenue $22.19B, +47.9% y/y; AI chip revenue +143%) — this is a financing-structure/leverage concern, a new and different vector of AI-trade risk than the capex de-rating I got wrong in July.

XLU: up only ~3.5% YTD, trailing PE ~23x vs a ~17x historical norm, badly lagging the narrower electrification/equipment funds. Checked against my own numbers: XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY — it is an absolute-positive, relative-negative leg until Sep-30, with the real edge in the Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (+1.24%, 19/26, 8/10 last decade). So I declined to add to it now despite the defensive rotation logic; that add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash.

EFA: EAFE continues to outperform US equity in 2026 in USD terms on European fundamentals, which is a headwind to the short, but the position is a 3% token.
